text:
maria: Quick update — ran perf + flamegraph on the CPU-side path for the new batching heuristic. Seeing a big tokenization hotspot when batch size > 8, spikes around ~120-200ms per request. Not expected.

devon: Interesting. Is that the Python tokenizer or the C extension?

maria: It's the Python wrapper we landed last week. We call the C tokenizer but there's a per-token Python loop for normalization.

ryan: Can you paste the perf command you used?

maria: Ran: 
```
sudo perf record -F 99 -a -g -- python3 -m myruntime.server --profile-load test_batch_12.json
sudo perf script | ./FlameGraph/stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded
./FlameGraph/flamegraph.pl out.folded > perf-flame.svg
```
Generated flame shows a big wedge labeled `py:tokenize.normalize_token` calling into `pyobject_getattr` etc.

alex: Did you try perf with LBR or callgraph off? Could be misleading if kernel frames are included.

maria: Yep tried -g and --no-builtin; still the Python frames dominate. I also ran a C-level capture with `perf record -e cpu-clock -g --call-graph dwarf` to get inline frames; same story.

devon: Any traces from perfetto/nsys on the GPU side? Maybe batching causes CPU scheduler churn while waiting on GPU.

maria: I have an nsys timeline: GPU is mostly idle waiting for pre/post processing when batch size grows. The CPU waits on locks in `batch_queue::pop()` then does tokenization. So two issues: serialized tokenization, and lock contention.

ryan: That matches earlier KV cache comments — if we re-use KV across requests we might serialize more. Is KV cache access protected by the same lock?

maria: Yes — we currently take the same global mutex for cache lookup and for queuing batches. I profiled with `perf annotate` and saw `pthread_mutex_lock` hot.

alex: Suggest we do a cheap experiment: move KV lookup before the queue lock and do a per-request short-circuit. Also try buffering tokenization in a background worker so enqueue is O(1).

devon: Also consider switching normalization to vectorized NumPy or a small C shim to push work off Python. If tokenization is dominantly Python-level, a C shim could drop 50-80% CPU.

maria: Agreed. I instrumented a microbenchmark: pure C tokenizer does ~3x tokens/sec vs Python wrapper. But integration work to avoid GC pauses is needed.

perf-bot: perf-run: completed 1758123600 — summary: total samples 2.1M, top symbols: py::normalize_token (28%), pthread_mutex_lock (15%), scheduler::dispatch (9%). See /tmp/perf-summary.txt

ryan: Nice. Can you upload the folded stacks and the flame svg? I'll check call paths. Also run with `perf record -e cpu-clock -g -- ./server --batcher-profile` to capture batching frames.

maria: Uploaded to `s3://redwood-infra/perf/1758123456/`. Flame svg + folded stacks + perf.data included.

alex: Another quick idea: adaptive batching — if tokenization per-request cost > threshold, cap batch size to reduce total tokenization work per wall time. Unusual but might improve latency tail.

devon: Good call. Also check Python GIL contention. If background tokenizers are threads, GIL will serialize them. Might need multiprocessing or a C extension that releases GIL.

maria: I'll prototype two paths: 1) move normalization into C shim (release GIL) and 2) background pool using multiprocessing + shared memory buffer for token arrays. Will iterate tomorrow.

ryan: When you have the microbench, also run `perf stat -e task-clock,cs,migrations,context-switches` to measure scheduler overhead per experiment. That will confirm if we lose time to context switching.

maria: Will do. Thanks for the suggestions. I'll update thread with results and a small flame svg diff. :thumbsup:
